questions.stem: A 45-year-old man collapses suddenly while running for a bus. There was no preceding lightheadedness, nausea, or sweating. He regained consciousness within 30 seconds but bruised his forehead. He mentions that his father died suddenly in his sleep at age 38. On examination in the emergency department, his pulse is 76 bpm, BP is 126/80 mmHg, and a 12-lead ECG shows T-wave inversion in leads V1-V4 and QTc 460 ms. Under UK NICE guidance (CG109), what is the most appropriate immediate management step?

choices.text: Discharge with reassurance that this was simple vasovagal syncope
Prescribe fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily and review in 3 months
Admit or urgently refer for specialist cardiovascular evaluation with telemetry/echocardiography
Arrange an outpatient head-up tilt table test in 6 months
Advise increasing dietary salt and oral fluid intake

questions.explanation: Distinguishing cardiac from non-cardiac syncope is crucial for risk stratification. This patient has multiple major high-risk red flags under NICE CG109: syncope during exertion (running), absence of prodrome, family history of premature sudden unexplained cardiac death (<40 years), and an abnormal 12-lead ECG. Such patients require urgent specialist cardiovascular assessment and inpatient telemetry/echocardiography to rule out arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy or channelopathy.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize high-risk red flags in syncope requiring urgent specialist cardiovascular evaluation.

citations.quote: Refer urgently for specialist cardiovascular assessment people with transient loss of consciousness who have red flag features: an ECG abnormality, syncope during exertion, family history of sudden cardiac death aged under 40.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Transient loss of consciousness ('blackouts') in over 16s
authoritative_guidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit with acute anterior myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock. His blood pressure is 74/46 mmHg, heart rate is 112 bpm, and serum lactate is 4.8 mmol/L. His extremities are cold and clammy, with oliguria. Bedside echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 25% with extensive anterior wall akinesis. Which of the following is the first-line vasopressor of choice to restore perfusion pressure in cardiogenic shock?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is the first-line vasopressor of choice in cardiogenic shock (predominantly alpha-1 vasoconstriction with modest beta-1 support). In the landmark SOAP II trial, dopamine was associated with a significantly higher rate of tachyarrhythmias and increased mortality compared to norepinephrine in cardiogenic shock. Phenylephrine lacks inotropic support and can impair cardiac output by increasing afterload without inotropic enhancement.
questions.learning_objective: Select norepinephrine as the evidence-supported first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock.

citations.quote: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock to restore perfusion pressure, combined with dobutamine as the initial inotrope for low cardiac output.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Management of Cardiogenic Shock: Clinical Review and Practice Recommendations
authoritative_guidelines.organization: European Society of Cardiology (ESC) / BCIS

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with ischemic cardiogenic shock has received norepinephrine infusion, achieving a mean arterial pressure of 68 mmHg. However, her cardiac index remains low at 1.7 L/min/m2, central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) is 52%, and urine output remains <0.3 mL/kg/h. Which of the following inotropic agents is the first-line choice to increase myocardial contractility and improve cardiac output in this patient?
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is the first-line inotropic agent in cardiogenic shock with persistent low cardiac output despite adequate perfusion pressure. Acting primarily as a beta-1 adrenergic agonist with mild beta-2 activity, it increases myocardial inotropy and produces moderate vasodilatation, enhancing cardiac index and organ perfusion. Milrinone is a second-line inodilator, while beta-blockers and diltiazem are contraindicated due to negative inotropy.
questions.learning_objective: Identify dobutamine as the first-line inotropic agent in cardiogenic shock with low cardiac output.

citations.quote: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock to restore perfusion pressure, combined with dobutamine as the initial inotrope for low cardiac output.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Management of Cardiogenic Shock: Clinical Review and Practice Recommendations
authoritative_guidelines.organization: European Society of Cardiology (ESC) / BCIS

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 2 hours of crushing central retrosternal chest pain, diaphoresis, and acute pulmonary edema. His ECG reveals acute ST-elevation in leads V1–V6. He is hypotensive with blood pressure 78/50 mmHg and cold extremities, consistent with cardiogenic shock complicating acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Which of the following therapeutic interventions has the strongest evidence for improving survival in AMI-induced cardiogenic shock?

choices.text: Routine intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) insertion without revascularisation
Therapeutic anticoagulation with enoxaparin alone followed by elective outpatient review
Emergent coronary revascularisation (primary percutaneous coronary intervention, PCI)

questions.explanation: Emergent coronary revascularisation by primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or CABG is the cornerstone of treatment that has proven to reduce mortality in patients with cardiogenic shock complicating acute myocardial infarction (SHOCK trial). Routine intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) placement failed to demonstrate a survival benefit in the IABP-SHOCK II trial and is not routinely recommended. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in acute cardiogenic shock.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize emergent coronary revascularisation (primary PCI) as the cornerstone intervention to reduce mortality in AMI cardiogenic shock.

citations.quote: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock to restore perfusion pressure, combined with dobutamine as the initial inotrope for low cardiac output.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Management of Cardiogenic Shock: Clinical Review and Practice Recommendations
authoritative_guidelines.organization: European Society of Cardiology (ESC) / BCIS

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a syncopal episode while walking in her garden. On examination, her heart rate is 34 bpm, and blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg. She feels dizzy and appears pale and diaphoretic. A 12-lead ECG demonstrates complete atrioventricular block (third-degree AV block) with a ventricular escape rate of 34 bpm. According to Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK) adult bradycardia management guidelines, what is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment while preparing for pacing?
questions.explanation: This patient has severe bradycardia with adverse features (syncope, hypotension 88/54 mmHg, diaphoresis). The RCUK bradycardia algorithm dictates immediate administration of atropine 500 mcg IV (repeatable every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg). If atropine is ineffective, second-line options include transcutaneous pacing or an inotrope/chronotrope infusion (isoprenaline or adrenaline). Adenosine, beta-blockers, and verapamil further suppress AV conduction and are contraindicated.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the RCUK bradycardia algorithm: administer atropine 500 mcg IV for symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features.

citations.quote: In patients with symptomatic bradycardia and life-threatening features, give atropine 500 micrograms IV.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Resuscitation Council UK Peri-arrest Bradycardia Algorithm 2025
authoritative_guidelines.organization: Resuscitation Council UK

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man collapses in the hospital outpatient corridor. The resuscitation team arrives immediately. He is unresponsive and apnoeic with no carotid pulse. The defibrillator pads are attached, and the rhythm check displays ventricular fibrillation. A first shock of 150 J biphasic is delivered, and CPR is resumed immediately for 2 minutes. At the second rhythm check, ventricular fibrillation persists, and a second shock is delivered followed immediately by 2 minutes of CPR. At the third rhythm check, ventricular fibrillation remains. A third shock is delivered. According to the Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK) Advanced Life Support guidelines, which medications should be administered during the CPR cycle immediately following the third shock?

choices.text: Adrenaline 1 mg IV and Amiodarone 300 mg IV
Atropine 3 mg IV and Calcium chloride 10 mL 10% IV
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV and Lignocaine 100 mg IV

questions.explanation: In the RCUK Adult Advanced Life Support algorithm for shockable rhythms (VF/pVT), after the 3rd shock, the resuscitation team administers adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV during the subsequent 2 minutes of CPR. Adrenaline is then repeated every alternate cycle (every 3–5 minutes), and a second dose of amiodarone (150 mg IV) is given after the 5th shock. Atropine is no longer used in cardiac arrest protocols.
questions.learning_objective: Recall medication administration timing in the RCUK ALS shockable algorithm (adrenaline 1mg and amiodarone 300mg post-3rd shock).

citations.quote: In shockable cardiac arrest, give adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV after the 3rd shock has been delivered and CPR resumed.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Adult Advanced Life Support Guidelines 2025
authoritative_guidelines.organization: Resuscitation Council UK

questions.stem: During an in-hospital resuscitation attempt for an adult in cardiac arrest, the team leader evaluates the quality of CPR being delivered. Which of the following chest compression metrics reflects high-quality adult cardiopulmonary resuscitation according to UK resuscitation standards?

choices.text: Compression rate of 80–90 per minute and depth of 3–4 cm to minimize rib fractures
Compression rate of 140–160 per minute with partial recoil to maintain coronary perfusion
Compression depth of 7–8 cm with continuous manual pressure between compressions
Compression rate of 100–120 per minute and depth of 5–6 cm with complete chest recoil
Compression-to-ventilation ratio of 15:2 with pauses of 15 seconds for pulse checks

questions.explanation: High-quality CPR requires a chest compression rate of 100–120 compressions per minute, a compression depth of 5–6 cm in adults, complete chest recoil after each compression, and minimization of interruptions in compressions. Leaning on the chest between compressions prevents complete recoil and significantly diminishes venous return and coronary perfusion pressure.
questions.learning_objective: Identify high-quality CPR metrics (rate 100-120/min, depth 5-6 cm, complete recoil) per RCUK guidelines.

citations.quote: For non-shockable rhythms (PEA or asystole), give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as venous access is achieved, and continue CPR 30:2.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Adult Advanced Life Support Guidelines 2025
authoritative_guidelines.organization: Resuscitation Council UK

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents to the emergency department with acute worsening of shortness of breath, wheezing, and increased production of green purulent sputum over the past two days. On arrival, his respiratory rate is 26 breaths/min, heart rate 98 bpm, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, and oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Arterial blood gas shows: pH 7.32, PaCO2 6.8 kPa (normal 4.7-6.0), PaO2 7.1 kPa (normal 10.0-14.0), HCO3 29 mmol/L (normal 22-26). Under UK guidelines (NICE NG115), what is the most appropriate initial oxygen delivery target?

choices.text: Target SpO2 94–98% using 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask
Target SpO2 98–100% using high-flow nasal cannula
Immediate room air without supplemental oxygen
Target SpO2 80–84% to avoid respiratory drive depression
Target SpO2 88–92% using a 28% or 24% Venturi mask

questions.explanation: In acute exacerbations of COPD, particularly when the patient is at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (demonstrated by PaCO2 6.8 kPa with baseline metabolic compensation), controlled oxygen therapy targeting an SpO2 of 88–92% via a 24% or 28% Venturi mask is mandatory under NICE NG115 and BTS guidelines. Uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen (e.g. 15 L non-rebreather mask targeting 94–98%) worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch and abolishes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, leading to severe hypercapnia and narcosis.
questions.learning_objective: Identify controlled oxygen target (88-92%) in acute COPD exacerbations with hypercapnic respiratory failure.

citations.quote: COPD is confirmed when post-bronchodilator spirometry demonstrates an FEV1/FVC ratio less than 0.70.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in over 16s: diagnosis and management
authoritative_guidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit with severe septic shock secondary to acute pyelonephritis. Within 24 hours of admission, she develops profound dyspnoea and worsening hypoxemia. Chest radiograph reveals extensive bilateral alveolar infiltrates sparing the cardiophrenic angles, without cardiomegaly. Echocardiography confirms normal left ventricular function and no evidence of left atrial hypertension. While receiving mechanical ventilation with PEEP of 10 cmH2O and FiO2 of 0.80, her arterial blood gas shows a PaO2 of 8.0 kPa (60 mmHg). Her PaO2/FiO2 ratio is 75 mmHg. According to the Berlin definition of ARDS, which severity category does this patient have?
questions.explanation: Under the Berlin criteria, ARDS severity is categorized by the PaO2/FiO2 ratio (with minimum PEEP >=5 cmH2O): Mild: 200 < PaO2/FiO2 <= 300 mmHg; Moderate: 100 < PaO2/FiO2 <= 200 mmHg; Severe: PaO2/FiO2 <= 100 mmHg. With a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 75 mmHg (60 / 0.80), this patient meets the criteria for severe ARDS.
questions.learning_objective: Classify ARDS severity based on PaO2/FiO2 ratio under the Berlin definition.

citations.quote: ARDS is defined by bilateral opacities on chest imaging not fully explained by effusions, and PaO2/FiO2 <= 300 with PEEP >= 5 cmH2O.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: The Berlin Definition
authoritative_guidelines.organization: ARDS Definition Task Force (JAMA)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old intubated man weighing 70 kg (predicted body weight 70 kg) with severe acute pancreatitis develops moderate ARDS. The intensive care team is adjusting his mechanical ventilator settings. In accordance with evidence-based lung-protective ventilation guidelines (FICM/ICS), which of the following tidal volume and airway pressure targets should be selected?

choices.text: Tidal volume 10–12 mL/kg actual body weight and plateau pressure < 45 cmH2O
Tidal volume 8–10 mL/kg predicted body weight without PEEP
Tidal volume 15 mL/kg to maximize alveolar recruitment
Plateau pressure maintained above 35 cmH2O to prevent derecruitment
Tidal volume 4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight and plateau pressure < 30 cmH2O

questions.explanation: Lung-protective ventilation is the cornerstone of ARDS management to minimize ventilator-induced lung injury (volutrauma and barotrauma). Standard guidelines mandate low tidal volume ventilation (4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight, or <=6 mL/kg PBW) and limitation of end-inspiratory plateau pressure to <30 cmH2O. High tidal volumes (10–12 mL/kg) significantly increase mortality in ARDS.
questions.learning_objective: Identify low tidal volume (4-6 mL/kg PBW) and plateau pressure (<30 cmH2O) targets in ARDS lung-protective ventilation.

citations.quote: Use low tidal volume ventilation targeted to 6 mL/kg predicted body weight in patients with ARDS.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Guideline for the Management of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
authoritative_guidelines.organization: Faculty of Intensive Care Medicine / Intensive Care Society (FICM/ICS)

questions.stem: A 46-year-old ventilated woman with severe ARDS secondary to bacterial pneumonia has persistent refractory hypoxaemia. Despite lung-protective ventilation (tidal volume 5 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure 28 cmH2O, PEEP 14 cmH2O, FiO2 0.85), her arterial blood gas shows a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 115 mmHg. According to FICM/ICS and international ARDS guidelines, which evidence-based non-pharmacological maneuver should be initiated?

choices.text: Prone positioning for at least 16 consecutive hours daily
Bilateral tube thoracostomy for prophylactic pleural drainage

questions.explanation: In patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio <150 mmHg despite optimal lung-protective settings, early prone positioning for at least 16 consecutive hours per day is strongly recommended. Prone positioning improves ventilation-perfusion matching, promotes dorsal lung recruitment, and has been demonstrated in landmark trials (PROSEVA) to significantly reduce mortality in severe ARDS. Routine HFOV is not recommended due to lack of survival benefit and potential harm.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize the indication (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg) and duration (>=16 hours/day) for prone positioning in severe ARDS.

citations.quote: Use low tidal volume ventilation targeted to 6 mL/kg predicted body weight in patients with ARDS.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Guideline for the Management of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
authoritative_guidelines.organization: Faculty of Intensive Care Medicine / Intensive Care Society (FICM/ICS)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old Afro-Caribbean man attends his GP surgery for a routine health check. His clinic blood pressure is 152/94 mmHg. A repeat measurement 10 minutes later is 150/92 mmHg. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) confirms an average daytime blood pressure of 146/90 mmHg. Urine dipstick is negative for protein, serum creatinine is 82 umol/L, and his 12-lead ECG is normal. According to UK clinical practice guidelines (NICE NG136), which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?
questions.explanation: Under NICE NG136 (Hypertension in adults), step 1 antihypertensive monotherapy for adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin of any age (without type 2 diabetes), or any adult aged 55 and over, is a calcium-channel blocker (CCB). ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred step 1 treatment only in adults aged under 55 who are not of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin.
questions.learning_objective: Select appropriate Step 1 antihypertensive pharmacotherapy based on age and ethnicity per NICE NG136.

citations.quote: Offer a CCB to adults with hypertension without type 2 diabetes of any age with Black African or African-Caribbean family origin or aged 55 and over.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management
authoritative_guidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old Caucasian man with newly diagnosed essential hypertension attends for medication review. His clinic blood pressure remains elevated at 158/98 mmHg despite 6 weeks of ramipril 5 mg once daily. He has no other comorbidities and normal renal function. In accordance with UK stepped-care guidance (NICE NG136), which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Switch from ramipril to losartan 50 mg daily
Add a calcium channel blocker (e.g. amlodipine 5 mg daily)

questions.explanation: According to NICE NG136 stepped-care guidance for hypertension, when blood pressure is uncontrolled on Step 1 monotherapy with an ACE inhibitor (in a non-Black patient aged <55), Step 2 treatment is the combination of an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) with a calcium channel blocker (CCB). Switching to an ARB (losartan) is only indicated if the patient develops an intolerable dry cough on an ACE inhibitor. Spironolactone is used at Step 4 for resistant hypertension when potassium is <=4.5 mmol/L. Doxazosin is an alternative Step 4 alpha-blocker.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize Step 2 combination therapy (ACEi/ARB plus CCB) in the NICE NG136 hypertension treatment algorithm.

citations.quote: If blood pressure is not controlled with step 1 treatment, offer step 2 combination therapy with a CCB and an ACE inhibitor or ARB.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management
authoritative_guidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension is diagnosed with newly discovered non-valvular atrial fibrillation on an ambulatory 24-hour ECG. She is asymptomatic with a heart rate of 78 beats/min. Her blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg, and echocardiography shows mild left atrial enlargement with a normal left ventricular ejection fraction (58%). She has no prior history of stroke, thromboembolism, or bleeding. According to UK clinical practice guidelines (NICE NG196), which of the following is the most appropriate stroke prevention strategy?

choices.text: Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel

questions.explanation: This patient's CHA2DS2-VASc score is 4 (Age 65-74 = 1, Female sex = 1, Hypertension = 1, Diabetes = 1). Under NICE NG196 guidelines, anticoagulation with a direct-acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC) such as apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban, or dabigatran is recommended for all women with a CHA2DS2-VASc score >=2 and men with score >=1. Aspirin or antiplatelet therapy is explicitly contraindicated as sole therapy for stroke prevention in AF due to lack of efficacy and similar bleeding risk.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate CHA2DS2-VASc stroke risk and select DOAC therapy over antiplatelet monotherapy in atrial fibrillation per NICE NG196.

citations.quote: Offer anticoagulation with a DOAC to people with atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or more.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management
authoritative_guidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the medical assessment unit with palpitations and mild fatigue over the past three weeks. Examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse at 128 beats/min and blood pressure 138/84 mmHg. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. He is clinically euvolemic with clear lung fields and no signs of heart failure. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological agent for rate control in this hemodynamically stable patient?
questions.explanation: Under NICE NG196 guidelines, rate control is the preferred initial strategy for patients with atrial fibrillation who are not hemodynamically unstable. A standard beta-blocker (such as bisoprolol or metoprolol) or a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) is the first-line therapy. Digoxin monotherapy is only recommended as first-line in sedentary patients or those with coexisting heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, as it is ineffective at controlling heart rate during exertion. Amiodarone is reserved for rhythm control or when other options fail.
questions.learning_objective: Identify standard beta-blockers as first-line rate control therapy in hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation.

citations.quote: Offer a standard beta-blocker (other than sotalol) or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker as initial monotherapy for rate control in atrial fibrillation.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management
authoritative_guidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic mitral stenosis is scheduled for routine dental scaling and cavity restoration. She asks whether she needs prophylactic antibiotics before her dental visit to prevent infective endocarditis. Under UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE CG64) guidance, what is the current recommendation regarding antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures?

choices.text: Oral amoxicillin 2 g should be taken 1 hour before every dental procedure
Antibiotic prophylaxis is NOT routinely recommended for dental procedures
Intravenous gentamicin and ampicillin are required 30 minutes prior
Oral clindamycin 600 mg is mandatory for all valvular heart disease patients
Dental procedures are strictly contraindicated in patients with heart valve disease

questions.explanation: Under UK NICE CG64 guidelines, routine antibiotic prophylaxis is explicitly NOT recommended for people at risk of infective endocarditis undergoing dental or non-dental interventional procedures. This is a classic UK-specific clinical practice point (in contrast to US AHA / European ESC guidelines). Patients are instead advised on maintaining meticulous oral hygiene and recognizing early symptoms of infective endocarditis.
questions.learning_objective: Recall the UK NICE CG64 guidance advising against routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures.

citations.quote: Three sets of blood cultures should be drawn from separate venipuncture sites before antimicrobial administration in suspected infective endocarditis.

authoritative_guidelines.title: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis
authoritative_guidelines.organization: European Society of Cardiology (ESC)

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman with exertional angina undergoes transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) for evaluation of a systolic murmur. Continuous-wave Doppler across the aortic valve demonstrates a peak aortic jet velocity (Vmax) of 4.3 m/s and a mean transvalvular pressure gradient of 44 mmHg. The calculated aortic valve area by the continuity equation is 0.8 cm2 (indexed AVA 0.45 cm2/m2). Left ventricular ejection fraction is 60%. According to international and UK NICE NG208 criteria, how should the severity of her aortic stenosis be classified?
questions.explanation: Severe aortic stenosis is defined echocardiographically by a peak aortic velocity (Vmax) >= 4.0 m/s, a mean transvalvular gradient >= 40 mmHg, and an aortic valve area (AVA) < 1.0 cm2 (or indexed AVA < 0.6 cm2/m2). With Vmax 4.3 m/s, mean gradient 44 mmHg, and AVA 0.8 cm2, this patient meets all hemodynamic criteria for severe aortic stenosis.
questions.learning_objective: Apply echocardiographic criteria (Vmax >4 m/s, mean gradient >40 mmHg, AVA <1.0 cm2) to define severe aortic stenosis.

citations.quote: The cardinal symptoms of severe aortic stenosis are exertional dyspnoea, angina, and syncope.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Heart valve disease in adults: investigation and management
authoritative_guidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with chronic ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 28%) is admitted for worsening pulmonary edema. Echocardiography shows severe functional mitral regurgitation secondary to left ventricular spherical remodeling. She is currently taking ramipril 2.5 mg and furosemide 40 mg daily. According to NICE heart failure guidelines (NG106) and valvular guidelines (NG208), what is the mandatory first-line strategy before considering invasive transcatheter or surgical mitral valve interventions for secondary/functional MR?

choices.text: Immediate urgent open-heart mechanical mitral valve replacement
High-dose oral steroid therapy for six months
Discontinuation of all ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers
Optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

questions.explanation: In functional mitral regurgitation (FMR), guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (including ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2i, plus cardiac resynchronization therapy if indicated) is the essential first-line foundation. Optimal medical therapy promotes reverse LV remodeling and can substantially diminish the severity of functional regurgitation. Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) or surgery is considered only if severe symptomatic MR persists despite optimal GDMT.
questions.learning_objective: Identify guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure as the mandatory initial management for functional mitral regurgitation.

citations.quote: In secondary (functional) mitral regurgitation, optimise guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction as first-line treatment.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Heart valve disease in adults: investigation and management
authoritative_guidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man achieves return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after 14 minutes of out-of-hospital CPR following a ventricular fibrillation arrest. On transfer to the intensive care unit, he remains comatose (Glasgow Coma Scale score 3, eyes not opening, no motor response). His 12-lead ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia with diffuse ST depression. What is the key target in post-resuscitation neuroprotective care regarding temperature management according to current resuscitation guidelines?

choices.text: Rapid induction of profound hypothermia targeting 28–30 °C
Routine rewarming to 38.5–39.0 °C to promote cerebral metabolism
Permissive hyperthermia up to 39.5 °C for 72 hours
No temperature monitoring or intervention required
Targeted temperature control strictly preventing fever (maintaining temperature <= 37.5 °C)

questions.explanation: Post-resuscitation care plays a crucial role in neurological outcome and recovery. Current RCUK and international guidelines recommend targeted temperature management (TTM) for comatose adult patients after ROSC, with the primary objective of actively preventing fever (temperature >37.7 °C) for at least 72 hours, maintaining normothermia (36.0–37.5 °C). Fever post-cardiac arrest is strongly associated with exacerbated cerebral injury and poor functional outcome.
questions.learning_objective: Outline post-resuscitation targeted temperature management principles to prevent post-arrest hyperthermia.

citations.quote: Actively prevent fever after cardiac arrest. Maintain a target temperature <= 37.5 °C in patients who remain comatose after ROSC.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Adult Advanced Life Support Guidelines 2025
authoritative_guidelines.organization: Resuscitation Council UK

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with established COPD attends an annual respiratory review. She currently uses an inhaled short-acting beta2-agonist (salbutamol) as needed but experiences persistent daily breathlessness (mMRC grade 2). She has had no exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids or hospitalisation in the past 12 months. She has no past history or features of asthma, and her blood eosinophil count is 0.08 x 10^9/L (low). In accordance with UK NICE NG115 guidelines, which of the following maintenance regimens is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Combination long-acting beta2-agonist plus long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LABA + LAMA)
Combination inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta2-agonist (ICS + LABA)
Triple therapy with LAMA + LABA + ICS

questions.explanation: Under NICE NG115, for patients with COPD who remain breathless on short-acting bronchodilators without asthmatic features or features suggesting steroid responsiveness (no asthma history, no blood eosinophilia), the recommended next step is dual bronchodilation with a LABA + LAMA. ICS-containing combinations (LABA + ICS or triple therapy) are reserved for patients with asthmatic features or those with high eosinophils and frequent exacerbations.
questions.learning_objective: Select LABA + LAMA dual bronchodilator therapy for breathless COPD patients without asthmatic features per NICE NG115.

citations.quote: In patients with COPD at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, titrate oxygen to achieve a target saturation of 88–92%.

authoritative_guidelines.title: BTS Guideline for oxygen use in healthcare and emergency settings
authoritative_guidelines.organization: British Thoracic Society (BTS)

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with COPD on dual bronchodilator therapy (umeclidinium/vilanterol) experiences two severe exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids and antibiotics over the preceding 6 months. His full blood count demonstrates a peripheral blood eosinophil count of 0.45 x 10^9/L (elevated, >300 cells/uL). Which of the following pharmacological adjustments is most indicated to reduce his future exacerbation frequency?

choices.text: Discontinue all long-acting bronchodilators and start oral roflumilast monotherapy
Escalate to triple therapy by adding an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) to his LABA/LAMA
Start long-term azithromycin 250 mg three times weekly without adjusting inhalers
Increase the dose of short-acting salbutamol to 8 puffs daily

questions.explanation: COPD exhibits treatable traits, and airway inflammation can be neutrophilic or eosinophilic. In patients suffering from recurrent exacerbations despite dual bronchodilation whose blood eosinophils are elevated (>300 cells/uL or >=0.3 x 10^9/L), escalating to triple therapy (LAMA + LABA + ICS) provides significant clinical benefit in reducing exacerbations and improving lung function.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize elevated blood eosinophils as a treatable trait indicating ICS escalation in frequent COPD exacerbators.

citations.quote: COPD is confirmed when post-bronchodilator spirometry demonstrates an FEV1/FVC ratio less than 0.70.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in over 16s: diagnosis and management
authoritative_guidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated in the hypertension clinic for persistent severe hypertension. Her clinic blood pressure is 168/104 mmHg despite adhering to amlodipine 10 mg and ramipril 10 mg daily. Basic blood investigations reveal serum sodium 143 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L (normal 3.5-5.0), and creatinine 74 umol/L. She takes no over-the-counter medications or herbal remedies. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial screening investigation for the suspected underlying cause of her secondary hypertension?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with treatment-resistant hypertension in a young adult accompanied by spontaneous hypokalemia (3.1 mmol/L), which strongly suggests primary aldosteronism (Conn's syndrome). The recommended initial screening test is the plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR). Fractionated metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma, which typically presents with paroxysmal headache, sweating, and palpitations. Renal Doppler evaluates renal artery stenosis, and urinary cortisol evaluates Cushing's syndrome.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the primary screening test for secondary hypertension caused by primary aldosteronism in a patient with hypokalemia.

citations.quote: In young patients with severe or resistant hypertension, screen for secondary causes including primary hyperaldosteronism.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presents with repeated episodes of lightheadedness and fainting when standing up from his armchair. His supine blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg with a heart rate of 72 beats/min. After standing for 3 minutes, his blood pressure drops to 118/70 mmHg, and he feels lightheaded, while his heart rate increases to 78 beats/min. He has no loss of consciousness today, and his 12-lead ECG is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed when standing results in a sustained reduction in systolic blood pressure of >=20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. Here, systolic BP fell by 30 mmHg (from 148 to 118 mmHg), reproducing the patient's symptoms. POTS is characterised by an exaggerated heart rate increase (>=30 bpm or >120 bpm) without a drop in blood pressure.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose orthostatic hypotension using postural blood pressure measurements and threshold criteria.

citations.quote: Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed when standing systolic BP falls by at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP falls by at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old retired judge presents with three episodes of sudden syncope over the past 2 months occurring while shaving his neck and turning his head. He has no prior cardiac history and his 12-lead ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without conduction delay. Under continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring, right carotid sinus massage is performed for 5 seconds. This produces ventricular asystole lasting 4.2 seconds and a systolic blood pressure drop of 55 mmHg, which reproduces his presenting symptoms. Which of the following is the diagnostic finding demonstrated by this test?
questions.explanation: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity/syndrome is diagnosed when carotid sinus massage (CSM) in patients with syncope reproduces symptoms accompanied by asystole >3 seconds (cardioinhibitory response) and/or a fall in systolic blood pressure >50 mmHg (vasodepressor response). Here, asystole lasted 4.2 seconds with a 55 mmHg BP fall, fulfilling both criteria for carotid sinus syndrome. Permanent pacemaker implantation is indicated for symptomatic recurrent cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome.
questions.learning_objective: Interpret carotid sinus massage diagnostic criteria (asystole >3s or BP fall >50 mmHg) for carotid sinus syndrome.

citations.quote: Carotid sinus massage is diagnostic if it induces asystole > 3 s or a fall in systolic BP > 50 mmHg.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man presents with a 4-week history of low-grade fluctuating fevers, night sweats, anorexia, and general malaise. On examination, he has a new harsh 3/6 pansystolic murmur at the cardiac apex and splinter hemorrhages in his nailbeds. Infective endocarditis is suspected. What is the most critical initial microbiological investigation required to satisfy the major Duke criterion prior to initiating antimicrobial therapy?

choices.text: A single random blood culture taken after starting broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
Throat swab and sputum culture for viral PCR
Urine antigen test for Legionella pneumophila
Three sets of blood cultures obtained from separate venipuncture sites with >=30 minutes between sets

questions.explanation: Blood cultures represent the crucial diagnostic tool for infective endocarditis and fulfill a primary major Duke criterion. Standard UK and international protocols mandate obtaining three sets of blood cultures from separate venipuncture sites prior to commencing antibiotic therapy, because antibiotic exposure rapidly yields culture-negative endocarditis (occurring in ~10% of cases). A single blood culture is insufficient to distinguish true bacteremia from skin contamination.
questions.learning_objective: Specify blood culture collection protocol (3 sets prior to antibiotics) as a major Duke criterion in suspected infective endocarditis.

citations.quote: Three sets of blood cultures should be drawn from separate venipuncture sites before antimicrobial administration in suspected infective endocarditis.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve replacement performed 3 years ago presents with persistent Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia and fever. A bedside transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) is performed but image quality is limited due to acoustic shadowing from the mechanical prosthesis, showing no obvious mobile vegetation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next imaging investigation to evaluate for prosthetic valve endocarditis and periannular complications?

choices.text: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging without contrast

questions.explanation: Transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is significantly more sensitive than transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) for detecting valvular vegetations, prosthetic valve dysfunction, and periannular complications (abscess, fistula, or pseudoaneurysm). TEE is mandatory in all patients with suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis, complicated native valve endocarditis, or when TTE is negative/inconclusive despite high clinical suspicion.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize indications for transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) in suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis.

citations.quote: Antibacterial prophylaxis against infective endocarditis is not recommended routinely for people undergoing dental procedures.

authoritative_guidelines.title: Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis: antimicrobial prophylaxis against infective endocarditis in adults and children undergoing interventional procedures

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man receives a standard dual-chamber pacemaker with right ventricular apical pacing (RVAP) for symptomatic high-grade AV block. One year later, he develops new exertional dyspnoea and bilateral leg edema. Echocardiogram reveals that his left ventricular ejection fraction has declined from 55% to 35% with marked intraventricular dyssynchrony. Which of the following long-term adverse effects of conventional right ventricular apical pacing explains this presentation?

choices.text: Pacing-induced cardiomyopathy due to ventricular dyssynchrony

questions.explanation: Right ventricular apical pacing (RVAP) induces an artificial left bundle branch block activation pattern, causing ventricular dyssynchrony, asymmetrical hypertrophy, and impaired left ventricular systolic function, termed pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. This occurs in 10–20% of patients with high percentages of RV apical pacing, prompting the development of physiological conduction system pacing techniques.
questions.learning_objective: Identify pacing-induced cardiomyopathy and ventricular dyssynchrony as potential complications of RV apical pacing.

citations.quote: Permanent pacemaker implantation is indicated in third-degree atrioventricular block.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with symptomatic Mobitz type II second-degree AV block is being assessed for permanent pacemaker implantation. The electrophysiologist discusses modern physiological pacing techniques, such as His-bundle pacing (HBP) and left bundle branch area pacing, compared to conventional right ventricular pacing (RVP). According to recent meta-analyses (Abdin et al., 2022), what clinical benefit is associated with physiological His-bundle pacing compared to conventional RVP?

choices.text: Elimination of the requirement for dual-chamber leads
Avoidance of any surgical pocket or generator implantation
Lower lead revision rates compared to apical leads
Lower risk of heart failure hospitalisation and new-onset atrial fibrillation

questions.explanation: In a meta-analysis comparing His-bundle pacing (HBP) to right ventricular pacing (RVP), Abdin et al. [2022] found that HBP was associated with a lower risk of heart failure hospitalisation, new-onset atrial fibrillation, and a reduction in pacing-induced ventricular dyssynchrony. By directly engaging the intrinsic His-Purkinje conduction system, physiological pacing preserves narrow QRS duration and synchronous ventricular activation.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize the clinical advantages of physiological conduction system pacing (lower HF hospitalisation and new AF) over conventional RVP.

citations.quote: Permanent pacemaker implantation is indicated in third-degree atrioventricular block.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man presents with progressive exertional breathlessness, occasional chest tightness on climbing stairs, and one recent episode of lightheadedness. Cardiovascular examination reveals a slow-rising carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur loudest at the right second intercostal space radiating to both carotids, with an inaudible second heart sound (absent A2). What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Aortic stenosis (AS) is the most common degenerative valvular disease in elderly individuals (affecting 10–15% over 80 years). The classic clinical triad consists of exertional dyspnea, angina, and syncope. Physical signs of severe AS include a slow-rising pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus), an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, and a soft or absent A2 component of S2.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose severe aortic stenosis from classic physical examination findings (slow-rising pulse, murmur radiating to carotids).

citations.quote: The cardinal symptoms of severe aortic stenosis are exertional dyspnoea, angina, and syncope.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old frail woman with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (mean gradient 46 mmHg, peak velocity 4.4 m/s) is reviewed by the multidisciplinary Heart Team. Her STS surgical mortality risk score is calculated at 8.5% (high surgical risk). She is being evaluated for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Which imaging modality is considered the gold standard reference technique for pre-procedural anatomical assessment, including aortic annulus sizing and vascular access evaluation for TAVI?
questions.explanation: Multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) is the reference technique for pre-procedural planning of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI/TAVR). It provides precise three-dimensional measurements of the aortic valve annulus, coronary ostial heights, calcification distribution, and evaluation of peripheral iliofemoral vascular access routes. Exercise stress testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS.
questions.learning_objective: Identify multidetector CT as the reference imaging technique for pre-procedural TAVI anatomical evaluation.

citations.quote: The cardinal symptoms of severe aortic stenosis are exertional dyspnoea, angina, and syncope.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with severe ischemic functional mitral regurgitation refractory to optimal medical therapy is discussed in the Heart Team meeting. The cardiac surgeons and cardiologists consider whether restrictive mitral valve annuloplasty repair or mitral valve replacement is more suitable. According to surgical series evaluating functional mitral regurgitation outcomes, what is the primary long-term clinical challenge associated with restrictive annuloplasty repair in patients with severe LV tethering and adverse remodeling?

choices.text: High rate of recurrent mitral regurgitation over long-term follow-up
Ineffectiveness of all subsequent oral diuretics
Requirement for lifelong high-dose warfarin anticoagulation

questions.explanation: The major limitation of restrictive mitral valve annuloplasty repair in functional mitral regurgitation is a significant rate of recurrent mitral regurgitation (observed in up to 30–50% of patients within 2 years in randomized CTSN trials), primarily driven by ongoing left ventricular remodeling and progressive leaflet tethering. Despite this risk, repair avoids prosthetic valve-related complications and has been associated with favorable operative recovery in selected cohorts.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize recurrent mitral regurgitation as the primary long-term challenge of annuloplasty repair in functional MR.

citations.quote: In secondary (functional) mitral regurgitation, optimise guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction as first-line treatment.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old tall, slender university student presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset left-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea that began 4 hours ago while watching television. He is speaking in full sentences. His respiratory rate is 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, pulse is 72 bpm, and blood pressure is 122/76 mmHg. Chest radiograph reveals a 2.5 cm rim of air at the level of the left hilum, consistent with a moderate primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP). Under the 2023 British Thoracic Society (BTS) pleural statement, what is the most appropriate initial management approach for this hemodynamically stable patient?

choices.text: Conservative observation with clinical monitoring and outpatient follow-up
Immediate insertion of a 28 Fr large-bore intercostal chest tube
Emergency needle thoracocentesis in the 2nd intercostal space

questions.explanation: The 2023 BTS Clinical Statement on Pleural Disease represents a paradigm shift toward conservative management for stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP). In a hemodynamically stable patient with minimal symptoms, conservative observation alone is safe and effective regardless of radiological pneumothorax size. Interventions such as needle aspiration or chest drain insertion carry procedural complications and are reserved for patients with significant dyspnea, physiological instability, or failure to resolve.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize conservative observation as an evidence-based initial strategy in stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax per BTS 2023.

citations.quote: In minimally symptomatic patients with primary spontaneous pneumothorax and no significant breathlessness, conservative management with observation alone is recommended.

authoritative_guidelines.organization: British Thoracic Society (BTS)

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with a moderate primary spontaneous pneumothorax is enrolled in a randomized trial comparing conservative observation to interventional chest drainage (Brown et al., NEJM 2020). What was the primary conclusion demonstrated by multicenter trials evaluating conservative observation versus interventional treatment in stable PSP?

choices.text: Conservative observation resulted in a 90% mortality rate and should never be used
Intervention with large-bore surgical thoracostomy is mandatory within 1 hour of diagnosis
Conservative observation was non-inferior to interventional management and associated with lower recurrence and fewer adverse events
Observation required four weeks of continuous inpatient bed rest
Only patients over 65 years of age benefit from conservative observation

questions.explanation: In the landmark multicenter trial by Brown et al. [2020] in moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax, conservative observation was found to be non-inferior to interventional drainage for radiographic resolution at 8 weeks, and was associated with significantly fewer hospital days, less time off work, and a substantially lower risk of pneumothorax recurrence. This evidence forms the basis of current BTS conservative guidelines.
questions.learning_objective: Summarize trial evidence supporting conservative observation over routine intervention in stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax.

citations.quote: In secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in patients over 50 years, chest drain insertion and admission is indicated.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation attends an outpatient cardiology clinic. He consumes approximately 35 units of alcohol per week and smokes 15 cigarettes daily. His BMI is 33 kg/m2. Despite taking flecainide and bisoprolol, he experiences weekly episodes of symptomatic palpitations lasting 2 to 4 hours. He is being evaluated for catheter ablation. Which of the following lifestyle modifications has the strongest evidence for reducing post-ablation AF recurrence and improving cardiovascular outcomes?

choices.text: Smoking cessation and reduction of alcohol intake
Strict adherence to a ketogenic diet
High-intensity interval training for two hours daily

questions.explanation: Smoking and excessive alcohol consumption both adversely affect AF outcomes and significantly increase the risk of post-ablation AF recurrence. Comprehensive lifestyle intervention and risk factor modification—including smoking cessation, limiting alcohol intake, weight loss, and screening for obstructive sleep apnea—are essential components of holistic AF management. Extreme exercise (high-intensity training) can actually trigger AF, and routine caffeine avoidance has not been shown to reduce AF recurrence.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize the critical role of lifestyle intervention (smoking cessation and alcohol reduction) in reducing AF recurrence.

citations.quote: Smoking and excessive alcohol consumption both adversely affect the incidence and progression of atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with previous anterior myocardial infarction and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 30%) develops moderate-to-severe functional mitral regurgitation (FMR). Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrates left ventricular dilatation, apical tethering of morphologically normal mitral valve leaflets, and an effective regurgitant orifice area of 0.28 cm2. What is the fundamental pathophysiological difference between functional (secondary) mitral regurgitation and degenerative (primary) mitral regurgitation?

choices.text: FMR is caused by congenital clefts in the anterior mitral leaflet
FMR results exclusively from acute bacterial destruction of the mitral valve annulus
FMR involves primary myxomatous degeneration and chordal rupture
FMR is caused by left ventricular remodeling and papillary muscle displacement with structurally normal leaflets
FMR only occurs in patients with normal left ventricular cavity dimensions

questions.explanation: In functional (secondary) mitral regurgitation (FMR), the mitral valve leaflets and chordae tendineae are structurally normal. The regurgitation is driven by left ventricular remodeling, annular dilatation, and papillary muscle displacement that cause apical and lateral leaflet tethering. In contrast, primary (degenerative) MR involves intrinsic structural leaflet/chordal disease (e.g. myxomatous degeneration, flail leaflet, or chordal rupture).
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the pathophysiology of functional mitral regurgitation (LV remodelling) from primary degenerative mitral disease.

citations.quote: In secondary (functional) mitral regurgitation, optimise guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction as first-line treatment.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old male smoker experiences sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Epidemiological studies indicate that primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) has a significantly higher admission incidence in young adult males compared to females. Which of the following predisposing factors is most strongly associated with the development of primary spontaneous pneumothorax?

choices.text: Congestive heart failure with fluid overload
Cigarette smoking and subpleural apical blebs/bullae
Deep vein thrombosis of the lower limb

questions.explanation: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) typically occurs in young, tall, slender individuals without overt clinical lung disease. Cigarette smoking increases the relative risk of PSP up to twenty-fold, and rupture of small subpleural apical blebs or bullae is the primary underlying anatomical cause. Heart failure, DVT, and GERD are not etiologic factors for PSP.
questions.learning_objective: Identify smoking and subpleural apical blebs as key etiologic factors in primary spontaneous pneumothorax.

citations.quote: Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency requiring immediate needle decompression prior to definitive chest tube insertion.
